content: When hemoglobin concentrations are above 80% of the cutoff levels, anemia is classified as mild. If hemoglobin levels fall between 80% and 60% of the cutoff, it is considered moderate anemia. Severe anemia is defined when hemoglobin levels are less than 60% of the cutoff. However, upon reviewing and recalculating the previous WHO cutoffs for anemia severity, it was found that the ranges were generally broader. For mild anemia, the range was between 85% and 92% of the cutoff value, while for severe anemia, it was between 62% and 70%. Considering the following factors: (i) the wide ranges used in previous calculations, (ii) the implications for initiating treatment based on anemia severity, and (iii) the comments from the Guideline Development Group (GDG) regarding implementation, the cutoff for severe anemia in children aged 6–23 months and women in their second trimester of pregnancy was retained at <70 g/L. For example, a hemoglobin level of 80 g/L in girls aged 12–17 years represents 67% of the cutoff of 120 g/L. Similarly, using 70 g/L as the cutoff for pregnant women in the second trimester corresponds to 67% of the cutoff of 105 g/L, which aligns well with the use of 70 g/L for pregnant women in the first and third trimesters, representing 64% of the cutoff of 110 g/L. For mild anemia, a hemoglobin level of 95 g/L is 90% of the cutoff of 105 g/L. The hemoglobin cutoffs to define anemia severity in individuals are as follows: For children aged 6–23 months: no anemia ≥105 g/L, mild anemia 95–104 g/L, moderate anemia 70–94 g/L, and severe anemia <70 g/L. For children aged 24–59 months: no anemia ≥110 g/L, mild anemia 100–109 g/L, moderate anemia 70–99 g/L, and severe anemia <70 g/L. For children aged 5–11 years: no anemia ≥115 g/L, mild anemia 110–114 g/L, moderate anemia 80–109 g/L, and severe anemia <80 g/L. For children aged 12–14 years (non-pregnant girls and boys): no anemia ≥120 g/L, mild anemia 110–119 g/L, moderate anemia 80–109 g/L, and severe anemia <80 g/L. For non-pregnant women aged 15–65 years: no anemia ≥120 g/L, mild anemia 110–119 g/L, moderate anemia 80–109 g/L, and severe anemia <80 g/L. For men aged 15–65 years: no anemia ≥130 g/L, mild anemia 110–129 g/L, moderate anemia 80–109 g/L, and severe anemia <80 g/L. For pregnancy: first trimester ≥110 g/L, second trimester ≥105 g/L, third trimester ≥110 g/L, with severe anemia defined as <70 g/L across all trimesters. The remarks and considerations for implementation, based on GDG discussions, include: The cutoffs were informed by a WHO-commissioned analysis of international databases containing hemoglobin and other biochemical and clinical indicators. These analyses calculated the 5th percentiles of hemoglobin distributions from healthy, ethnically diverse populations, predominantly from high-income settings in Australia, China, Europe, North America, and South America. Additional data from lower-income settings reported heterogeneous but generally lower 5th percentile values in participants without biochemical evidence of iron or vitamin A deficiencies or inflammation. However, due to the high burden of infections and inflammation in these settings, and the lack of definitive evidence to exclude their residual effects on hemoglobin concentration, these data were not included in the pooled analysis. The GDG decided to retain the cutoff of 130 g/L for men after considering concerns about the implications of iron therapy for males, the limited evidence, and the potential unintended consequences of changing the cutoff, such as initiating iron supplementation programs in men. The management of individuals with mild, moderate, or severe anemia may vary depending on the clinical scenario and the underlying causes of anemia. A clear association between anemia severity and clinical or statistical outcomes would be valuable for classifying anemia severity at the clinical or individual level and would help in the prevention and treatment of anemia. Further considerations include: Establishing optimal criteria to define a healthy population using statistical approaches. Conducting future studies to prospectively define 5th percentiles in healthy populations across all geographical regions, including infants and individuals aged >65 years. The GDG judged that reviewing hemoglobin cutoffs to define anemia and its severity could improve decisions about implementing public health interventions and treating anemia at the individual level. Harmonized, evidence-based guidelines for hemoglobin cutoffs would ensure equitable access to the same definition of anemia worldwide. While no studies specifically addressed costs, acceptability, and feasibility implications, the GDG considered that reviewing hemoglobin concentration cutoffs to define anemia was acceptable and feasible to key stakeholders, as improved cutoffs would benefit patients globally across clinical, laboratory, public health, and research settings. Regarding adjustments for external factors: Hemoglobin cutoffs should be adjusted for elevation of residence and/or smoking, as these factors significantly affect hemoglobin concentrations. For example, adjustments for elevation are recommended to diagnose anemia in individuals and populations, accounting for the effect of living at higher altitudes on hemoglobin levels. A common set of hemoglobin adjustments across age groups is likely appropriate and practical for elevations below 2500 m, where more than 98% of the world’s population resides. At elevations above 2500 m, adjustments may vary more by region due to known epigenetic differences. Research gaps include: The need for more data from a greater number of countries and population groups (e.g., infants, pregnant women, men, and older individuals) to confirm whether and to what extent regionand ethnicity-specific adjustments are required. Understanding differences in observed hemoglobin concentrations among populations with gene variants limiting hemoglobin production or maintenance, or those with epigenetic adaptations to living at very high elevations (>2500 m). Addressing the nuances of adjusting hemoglobin for elevation between different ethnicities within a region. The GDG considered the current evidence on the effects of adjusting hemoglobin concentrations by elevation to be of moderate quality, as data and modeling for elevations above 3000–3500 m were obtained from limited samples, mainly from Central and South America.
